I'm referencing the economic freedom of the world index by the Fraser Institute. I know the economists who put it together and I can assure you that all the Koch bros. money in the world wouldn't change the index. They measure across three areas: (1) size of government, (2) Security of Property Rights (3) Access to Sound Money (4) Freedom to Trade Internationally and (5) Regulations. A couple years back they did an accounting of all the research that has been conducted using the index. There's literally only a handful of bad outcomes that are associated with economic freedom.

I suppose my preferred 'system' would be one that a) accounts for dispersed knowledge and b) aligns incentives. From what I've seen, the more centralized a system becomes the more inadequately it deals with knowledge and incentive problems. For example, large democracies suffer from incentive problems; concentrated benefits to interest groups and dispersed costs to disinterested voters. So a governmental structure that I might endorse would be poly-centric. Many governments in competition with each other.

What would the policies be? They can vary. Ideally, the more options, the less individuals will be subjected to the will of others.

the more centralized a system becomes ...

On this point, we can find an important area of agreement. A "system" would apply to both government and business entities. If we break up governments and leave corporations intact, we will not disperse power. Rather, we will shuffle it. Worse yet, if we put governments in official competition, we formalize the "race to the bottom" concept.

"Race to the bottom" is a very real and very basic concept. We either accept it and move to the next step, or we reject it and end at a low level of ideology. The concept says that when governments are in competition, large players -- businesses -- will extract every advantage from them.

I like Richard Wolff and I am not a socialist. I have found that socialists generally do the best criticisms of the economic system, but I am only willing to go so far to agree with their solutions. We need a mixed system, not an ideology. :)

I've heard this argument before, but it isn't grounded in any economic theory. Corporations face decreasing returns to scale, and inefficiency is kept in check by investors. Prices are a mechanism for dissemination of dispersed knowledge; the solution to the knowledge problem. This is why markets are important... prices are used to signal scarcity and subjective value. Profit and loss are a mechanism for solving the incentive problem. In free trade, an entrepreneur can only profit by providing others with value. Non-coercive trade is by default mutually beneficial. Government, which is centralized in a different way, does not benefit a) from market based prices and b) the feedback mechanism of profit and loss. Governments do not have the feedback mechanism of profit and loss and therefore no way to determine whether they are providing value. Absent profit and loss incentives the incentive problem arises; this is how you see things like regulatory capture.

Moreover, the fact that governments are easily captured by interest groups (corporations included) is a flaw of government, not of corporations. I see poly-centrism as a next best solution to our current governmental structure... by no means perfect but perhaps better.
